edits.walkthrough_append: Worked check: separate the two colonial types by asking who came to stay — in Australia and North America Europeans settled the land itself, displacing indigenous peoples; in India and Africa Europeans ruled from trading posts and garrisons over much larger subject populations. Same empire, two systems, two consequences. For the board examination, settler-colony questions ask you to define the category, name two colonies and their metropoles, and contrast the fate of native populations with that of subject peoples in non-settler colonies — the comparison, not the definition, carries the marks.

Worked check: weigh the debate's two claims against its evidence — Windschuttle argued frontier killings in Tasmania were few and poorly documented; his critics (Quadrant's opponents, the historians of the 'killing fields' school) replied with documentary tallies of massacres and the near-annihilation of the Tasmanian Aboriginal population. The quarrel was over numbers, but also over who may write national history. For the board examination, a question on the history wars expects the two positions with their authors, the stake — national memory and guilt — and the historiographical lesson that evidence is read within political present concerns.

Worked check: name the policies and count their effects — land seizure destroyed the economic base; residential schools and boarding institutions separated children from language and kin; bans on ceremony and language attacked the cultural core; reserves and forced relocations disciplined movement. The result across North America and Australia was communities fighting for survival of identity as much as life. For the board examination, native-fate questions require the policy list tied to consequences, one named institution or act as evidence, and the closing distinction between assimilation as policy and its outcome as cultural destruction.

Worked check: read Fukuzawa through one idea — 'national independence through civilisation': he held that Japan must learn Western science, institutions and manners not to imitate the West but to resist it, and his essays persuaded samurai and merchants alike; his textbooks taught a generation. For the board examination, questions on Meiji intellectuals ask who Fukuzawa was, what 'leaving Asia' or Western learning meant in his writing, and how his schools (Keio) served the modernising state — anchor each answer in one quotation or one institution so the essay has evidence, not just opinion.

Worked check: date the discovery in three steps — Charles Masson and others notice Harappa's ruined mounds and report bricks; Alexander Cunningham, the first Director-General of the ASI, sketches the site in the 1850s-70s and misses its age; then in 1921 Daya Ram Sahni excavates Harappa and in 1922 Rakhaldas Banerji Mohenjodaro, and John Marshall announces to the world a civilisation older than the Mesopotamian contact dates suggested. For the board examination, discovery questions are graded on this sequence with dates and names — the long delay between noticing and recognising is itself the standard interpretive point.

Worked check: read one plan like an engineer — at Mohenjodaro the settlement divides into citadel (west, higher) and lower town (east); streets run in a grid along cardinal directions; covered drains run beneath the sidewalks; the Great Bath sits within a walled precinct; wells serve individual houses. Each feature implies a decision — standardised bricks, planned drainage, water management — and taken together, a central authority capable of coordinating them. For the board examination, town-planning answers draw a small labelled sketch and interpret three features; the interpretation lines, not the labels, carry the marks.

Worked check: test each guess about the citadel against its evidence — the Great Bath suggests ritual function, the warehouse on the citadel at Lothal suggests storage and administration, the elevation itself suggests defence or precedence; yet no palace or temple has been found, so all readings remain arguments from use. State the uncertainty and you answer better than with a guess. For the board examination, citadel-versus-lower-town answers describe both sectors — building, elevation, construction — and then weigh two functions for the citadel's structures, closing that the absence of unmistakable public buildings keeps the question open.

Worked check: follow one craft through its chain — carnelian from Gujarat's pits was flaked, ground, drilled with fine steatite or copper drills and polished into the classic etched beads found from Harappa to Mesopotamia; shell from the coast was cut into bangles and inlays; faience was pressed into moulds. The distribution of finished beads maps the trade as surely as any text. For the board examination, craft-production answers name two crafts with their raw-material sources, describe one chaîne opératoire (sequence of steps), and close on what workshops and waste pieces tell the archaeologist about organisation.

Worked check: read the granaries and the bones together — massive brick granaries and threshing floors at Harappa imply grain collected from a wide countryside; charred wheat and barley remains, and cattle bones (the humped zebu) in the refuse, identify the staples; the terracotta plough model and the fire-alters at Kalibangan suggest tillage and ritual. For the board examination, agriculture questions are answered in evidence-pairs — remain plus implication (granary means surplus; plough model means tillage) — and the closing line that a city cannot feed itself: the countryside's grain was the civilisation's invisible base.

Worked check: weigh the three explanations against the evidence — climate shift and the weakening monsoon (palaeoclimate records), the Ghaggar-Hakra's drying ( vanished settlements along its bed), and river shifts undercutting agriculture; note what the evidence does not show — no mass graves, no conquest layer, no single catastrophe. Decline was a fade, not a fall: de-urbanisation, the drift eastward. For the board examination, decline questions expect the multi-cause answer, each cause tied to its kind of evidence, and the closing sentence that 'end' means the end of cities, not of people.

Worked check: follow the decipherment as a chain — Prinsep studies copies of inscriptions from across India; two scripts, Brahmi and Kharoshthi, repeat the same phrase; comparison with later Indo-Greek bilingual coins cracks the names; the recurring royal title 'devanampiya piyadasi' (beloved of the gods, of pleasing appearance) resolves into Ashoka when a Maski inscription names him outright. For the board examination, decipherment questions ask for the year, the method (bilingual coins, repeated formulae), and the consequence — Ashoka's edicts became readable, and Indian political history gained its first named voice.

Worked check: build the empire's story from three kinds of evidence — literature (the Arthashastra and the Mudrarakshasa name Chandragupta and his overthrow of the Nandas), epigraphy (Ashoka's edicts map the empire from Kandahar to Karnataka), and archaeology (Ashokan pillars, the Pataliputra palisade). Each source corrects the others; each alone misleads. For the board examination, an empire-overview answer runs founder-expansion-administration-decline with one evidence citation per stage, and closes on the historiographical point: the Mauryas are the first empire we can outline because their traces survive in three media at once.

Worked check: classify the inscriptions before quoting them — pillar edicts, major and minor rock edicts, cave inscriptions and the label inscriptions; then read one closely: Rock Edict XIII names Kalinga's war, the dead and deported, and the remorse that turned the king to dhamma — conquest renounced in the victor's own words. For the board examination, inscription answers carry the classification, the language and script (Prakrit in Brahmi, with Kharoshthi and Aramaic at the margins), and one edict read for content and purpose — the reading, not the list, is what the examiner rewards.

Worked check: test the Arthashastra as evidence — its chapters on revenue, spies, mines and the seven limbs of the state match the Mauryan machinery we see in the edicts and in Megasthenes' account, yet the text's date is argued (Mauryan core, later additions), so it is best used as the theory of kingship beside the practice of it. For the board examination, Arthashastra answers state the authorship tradition (Kautilya, Chandragupta's minister), name three of its concerns (taxation, espionage, administration), and end with the source-criticism line: a manual of ideals, priceless but not a newspaper.

Worked check: sort the sixteen by constitution and strength — monarchies such as Magadha, Kosala and Vatsa ruled by hereditary kings; oligarchies or ganas ruled by assemblies of elders; and Magadha's rise (Bimbisara and Ajatashatru) traced through three advantages: iron in the south Bihar forests, the fertile mid-Ganga plain, and elephants and rivers for war and trade. For the board examination, mahajanapada answers name the six most important with capitals, distinguish monarchy from gana, and explain Magadha's rise through the three advantages — the 'why Magadha' paragraph is the question's usual target.

Worked check: read a gana's constitution like a charter — the Buddha's own Shakya clan and the Lichchhavis of Vaishali ran councils of rajas, debated in assembly halls, and voted by procedures the texts describe; policy needed the elders' consent, and Dissent walked out. Compare with a monarchy: one ruler, one succession. For the board examination, gana-sangha answers define the oligarchic form, name two examples, explain why Buddhist and Jaina texts praised them (both religions rose in these polities' debate culture), and close with why monarchies ultimately won: concentrated resources for war.

Worked check: order the three on one timeline — Pushyamitra Shunga's coup ends the Mauryas (about 185 BCE); the Kanva wait a century and fall; the Satavahanas, rising in the Deccan, outlast both into the third century CE, their coins naming kings and their land grants charting Brahmanical expansion. For the board examination, a post-Mauryan answer states each dynasty with dates, capitals and one achievement — Shunga patronage of Sanskrit, Satavahana land grants and trade ports — and the closing line that regional powers, not one successor, inherited the Mauryan space.

Worked check: follow one group's track and transformation — the Shakas descend the Central Asian corridor, one branch settles in western India where the Kshatrapa kings strike dated coins that anchor Indian chronology; the Indo-Greeks before them mint the first portrait coins and patronise Buddhism (Menander); the Kushanas after them knit Central Asia to the Ganga plain and the Silk Road. Each wave became an Indian dynasty in time. For the board examination, Central Asian questions ask for the sequence, one coin or inscription evidence per group, and the closing theme: invasion into absorption, trade and art in the wake.

Worked check: date the urbanisation by its artefacts — Northern Black Polished Ware in the layers, punch-marked coins in the bazaars, and the texts (the Pali Jatakas) naming six great cities: Kashi, Kosala's Sravasti, and Magadha's Rajagaha among them. Cities mean surplus food, craftsmen, merchants and coinage, and each appears in the record together. For the board examination, second-urbanisation answers give the period, the evidence triad (NBPW, coins, texts), the city list, and the causes paragraph — iron agriculture's surplus and the Ganga trade — that links town and countryside.

Worked check: read a coin like a document — punch-marked silver pieces with solar and animal symbols speak for institutional issue; Indo-Greek portraits give kings' faces and dates; Kushana gold proclaims empire; Satavahana coins name rulers their inscriptions confirm, and ship motifs on some speak of the western trade. Weight standards (mashaka, karshapana) chart the monetary system's grammar. For the board examination, coinage answers trace the sequence punch-marked to Gupta gold, name two dynastic coins with one detail each, and close that coins are evidence twice over — for economy and for political history.

Worked check: follow the iron chain — an iron ploughshare cuts the heavy Ganga clay; wet rice in the transplanted paddies multiplies yield per field; wells, tanks and canals stretch the water; and the surplus feeds towns, monks and kings, who in return record land grants to open the forests further. Each link pulls the next. For the board examination, agricultural-expansion answers run this chain in order with one evidence each (finds of ploughshares, texts on irrigation, donative inscriptions), and close on the social consequence: hierarchies of landholding and the rise of the shudra cultivator's world.

Worked check: explain the method in three moves — collect every Sanskrit and regional version of the epic from across the subcontinent; compare them verse by verse; print the verses common to most manuscripts as the critical text and relegate the variants to an apparatus of footnotes. The result: a 'least common denominator' Mahabharata of about 75,000 verses against the Vulgate's 100,000. For the board examination, critical-edition answers give the institute, the years, the method in this three-move form, and the interpretive consequence — what every version shared may be the epic's oldest core.

Worked check: read the growth marks in the text itself — the core war-narrative speaks an older idiom; the Bhagavadgita's theology and the anushasana didactic books speak later ones; the list of redactions (Vyasa's composition, Vaishampayana's recital, the sutas' performance) mirrors layers of transmission from court to village. For the board examination, authorship questions expect the traditional three-stage account, the archaeological-textual dating (composition perhaps from about 500 BCE, closure early centuries CE), and the closing argument that the epic is less a book than a moving, growing archive of its centuries.

Worked check: read the episode as a debate — Draupadi's polyandrous marriage shocks the court; Yudhishthira cites ancestral precedent; the mother Kunti's word settles it; and later texts moralise the episode uneasily, some justifying, some explaining away. Polyandry appears in the epic as practicable, in the law-books as problematic — the tension is the evidence. For the board examination, questions on Draupadi's marriage expect the narrative outline, the law-book contrast, and the historical argument that the epic preserves social practices the later prescriptive texts sought to discipline — epic as social history.

Worked check: map each varna to its stated duty — Brahmana: teach and sacrifice; Kshatriya: protect and rule; Vaishya: farm, trade, lend; Shudra: serve the other three — and then ask who assigns the duties: the Dharmasutras, authored within the top varnas, present a hierarchy of birth, not achievement. Women are placed beside the shudra in several prescriptions: no Veda, no independent sacrifice. For the board examination, varna answers state the four orders with functions, cite one prescription each from the texts, and close with the critical line that these are ideals of a literature, contested by the evidence of practice.
